name: Ferruginous
lede: Ferruginous means rust-colored, from the Latin for rust, and describes the reddish brown of iron-bearing earths and stones.

sections.title: The color of rust
sections.body:
Paterson defines ferruginous as the color of iron rust, a reddish brown, and gives the Latin root *ferrugin-* for rusty [1]. He lists a related compound, fusco-ferruginous, for a dark rust [2], and sends the plain color word iron back to ferruginous [3]. It is mainly a describer's word, used for rocks, plants, feathers and soils.

In pigment books the word keeps turning up as a plain adjective for iron-rich earth. Church wrote in 1901 that one kind of Vandyke brown was made by calcining ferruginous earths or brown ochres [4]. Salter (1869) called Verona brown a native ferruginous earth, while Toch (1916) called the name a fancy label for a mix of burnt umber with burnt or raw sienna [5]. Books disagree here, and by 1928 Heaton thought the name obsolete [5].

sections.title: A word hidden in a place name
sections.body: The Pigment Compendium records a guess that the French ochre name *ocre de rue* meant ochre from brooks of ferruginous waters, which Mérimée proposed in 1830 [6]. It is one proposed origin, not a settled one [6]. For the family see [[ochre]], [[sienna]], [[umber]] and [[rust]].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The earliest record of the name in our sources is Ridgway's color book of 1886, with later entries in Maerz and Paul (1930) and the ISCC-NBS system (1955) [7]. The swatch is a warm brick brown, near [[terracotta]] and [[reddish-brown]] [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This color appears in 433 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, 1.82%, as photographed [8]. In 82% of the 321 paintings where it is measured within the painting, it plays an accent [8]. It peaks in the 1300s, at 4.4% of 251 paintings, or 2.0 times the expected rate [8]. Amedeo Modigliani has it in 4 of 18 works, and Nepal is the most over-represented country at 5.3 times, from 6 of 25 paintings [8]. In printed English the adjective peaks in the 1850s [8]. A match in an aged photograph is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test [8].

questions.q: In most paintings that contain it, what role does this color play?

openers: Ferruginous is Latin for rusty, and in paintings it is mostly a small accent, not the main color.
